To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) fairness is no longer a sufficient condition for the optimal design of congestion controls for inelastic traffics; 2) fairness should be redefined to include the notion of admission control for inelastic flows; 3) at the aggregate level, a balance between elastic traffic and inelastic traffic should be maintained.

(a) fairness is a useful concept for elastic flows, (b) fairness is not necessarily useful for inelastic flows, and (c) a balance between elastic flows (which are fair) and inelastic flows (which are unfair) can maximize the network's overall utility.

1) fairness congestion control on an individual flow level is not always the best choice for inelastic flows, and 2) a balance between elastic traffic and inelastic traffic is still a good choice at the aggregate level.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of traffic control mechanisms that are fair, efficient, and robust to different workloads.
the fairness of traffic controls for elastic and inelastic flows in best-effort networks.
developing a methodology for comparing and evaluating the utility of traffic controls in the Internet.

fairness is not the best criterion for traffic control.

fairness of congestion control should be redefined in the presence of inelastic flows, while fairness of admission control should still be maintained.
